NPAPI which is what old flash, and most all other plugins like adobe reader, java, silverlight use, is very old (started with netscape in 1995). Newer technology is around and it's time to move forward. In the case of PPAPI, chrome's replacement for NPAPI, plugins can now be sandboxed instead of having direct access to the system (security hole).

It benefits Google by disabling products owned by their competitors. It's anti-competitive, practically the definition thereof, to use a product where one has market share to disrupt the business of another product.

What's going on is Google is pushing a new standard, whatever the benefits, and /disabling/ the old one. It's not as though they are saving some huge amount of space or resources to accomplish this - it's just because they want to. This is a power move and nothing more. It would be trivial to disable by default, yet leave the functionality for those who wish or need to use it for some reason. Yes, they say it will prevent crashes and such, but why does the browser maker care? It's not their computer that is crashing.

Unless, that is, Google has an invested interest in this. Which of course they do.

My point is not that NPAPI is good or something, or that PPAPI is inferior or that plug-ins are desirable. My point is that they exist, and frequently used, and their continued existence in legacy form harms no one.
